content: The word etrog (also pronounced as ethrog or esrog) originates from the Hebrew word אֶתְרוֹג, which is the most common term for the citron fruit, scientifically known as Citrus medica. This fruit is one of the four species used in the Jewish ritual of waving during the holiday of Sukkot. The other three species are the lulav (date palm frond), hadass (myrtle bough), and aravah (willow branch). In Leviticus 23:40, the etrog is referred to as pri etz hadar (פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר), which translates to a fruit of the beautiful tree. In modern Hebrew, the term hadar is associated with citrus, aligning with the rabbinical identification of the etrog as the fruit mentioned in the Torah. However, the commentary of Nahmanides suggests that hadar was originally the Hebrew word specifically for the citron, which was later replaced by etrog. The term etrog in Talmudic Aramaic conveys meanings of love and attraction and was adopted in Babylonia after the destruction of the First Temple. The Arabic name for the fruit, itranj (اترنج), is linguistically related to the Hebrew term. The itranj is also mentioned favorably in Islamic Hadith. Similar names, such as turunj, appear in various languages. Etrog trees are typically propagated from cuttings that are two to four years old, and the tree begins to bear fruit around the age of three. If grown from seeds, the tree will not produce fruit until approximately seven years of age, and genetic changes may occur in the tree and its fruit when seed propagation is used. The fruit is ready for harvest when it reaches about six inches in length, which is optimal for marketing purposes. It is usually picked while still green. The inner rind of the etrog is significantly thicker than the pulp, and the outer surface is somewhat hard and aromatic. The pulp is generally dry and can range in taste from sweet to strongly acidic, depending on the variety. According to Halakha (Jewish law), an etrog used for the mitzvah of the four species must be largely unblemished and possess an aesthetically pleasing form and shape. Special care is required during cultivation to avoid scratches from leaves and thorns. The bearing branch should be curved to encourage the fruit to grow straight downward; otherwise, the fruit may develop a curve due to its increasing weight. An etrog with a pitom (a structure at the tip composed of a style, called dad in Hebrew, and a stigma, called shoshanta) is considered especially valuable. However, varieties that naturally shed their pitom during growth, like other citrus species, are also kosher. Even if the stigma breaks off after harvest, the etrog can still be considered kosher as long as part of the style remains attached. Some Hasidic communities have a custom of selecting an etrog with a gartel (an hourglass-like waist around the middle), though Talmudic sources do not comment on this practice. The marketability of an etrog depends on its shape, cleanliness, and the condition of its apex. Some authorities hold that an etrog should not be taken from the cuttings of a grafted tree. The primary mitzvah involving the etrog is to hold it along with the other three species during the Hallel prayer on Sukkot. After the holiday, some people boil the peel of the etrog to make jam, fruit cake, or candied fruit. Others slice the etrog thinly and add it to vodka to create a unique beverage. There is an Ashkenazic tradition of eating the etrog on Tu B'Shevat, the New Year for Trees, to maximize the variety of fruits consumed on that day in praise of the Creator and to pray for a clean, non-grafted, and non-hybridized etrog for the next Sukkot. In the secular world, there is some confusion regarding the etrog. The variety originating from Corfu Island, which is now a leading cultivar in Israel, is often exclusively referred to as etrog for use in Jewish rituals. This naming convention was influenced by the botanical classification of the variety, known as variety etrog. However, the use of the Corfu variety has been historically disputed, as have its descendants in Israel. Nevertheless, many varieties have traditionally been used for the Feast of Tabernacles and may even be recommended. A general DNA study conducted by Professor E. Goldschmidt and colleagues, renowned researchers of the etrog, confirmed the genetic purity and relatedness of 12 known citron accessions. This study did not involve grafting, which is not believed to alter genetic material. Documentation of this study can be found in the Global Citrus Germplasm Network. In popular culture, the purchase of a beautiful (and often expensive) etrog plays a significant role in the plot of the film Ushpizin.
